The afternoon light, though softened by the heavy curtains, still found its way to illuminate the dust motes dancing lazily in Mrs. Pemberton’s drawing-room, a spectacle Mr. Finch seemed to find quite as engaging as the conversation. He had been discoursing at some length upon the merits of various horticultural pursuits, a topic Mrs. Pemberton had, with her usual enthusiasm, encouraged. Miss Eleanor Vance, however, found her attention drawn more to the subtle interplay of expressions between the speaker and his hostess than to the intricate details of rose cultivation.

“It is a peculiar joy,” Mr. Finch began again, adjusting his cravat with a somewhat unnecessary flourish, “to find oneself in such an agreeable assembly after a morning spent wrestling with accounts. One’s faculties, I assure you, are quite enlivened by the contrast, much like a parched soil after a refreshing rain.” He smiled, a rather too practiced expression, Miss Vance thought, and leaned slightly forward in his chair; his manner suggested an eagerness that verged on presumption.

“Indeed, Mr. Finch,” she replied, her voice soft but firm, for she felt a certain obligation to redirect his focus, “the mundane aspects of life do make these moments of relaxation all the more cherished. Though I confess, I have found even the most strenuous of tasks can be enlivened by good company, or at least by the promise of it.”

Mrs. Pemberton, who had been attending to a rather chipped teacup, now interjected with her usual vivacity. “Oh, my dear Mr. Finch, you are too modest! Your accounts, I am certain, are marvels of precision, not tedious at all. And Miss Vance, you are ever so charitable in your assessment of ordinary matters. My own accounts, I assure you, are a constant source of terror; Lady Ashworth knows, she has seen the state of my ledgers, and has often been so very kind as to offer her invaluable advice, though I fear it is quite wasted upon my poor, bewildered brain.”

Lady Ashworth, a woman of formidable presence who usually spoke little, now lowered her embroidery with a faint rustle of silk. “Mrs. Pemberton, you exaggerate, as ever. My advice, I trust, is never wasted, though its application may sometimes be delayed. Miss Vance speaks with sense, however. There is much to be gained from a diligent application to one’s duties, whatever their nature.” She spoke with an air of finality, and Mr. Finch, sensing perhaps that the general pronouncements were not leading to the sort of particular attention he craved, turned his full regard back to Miss Vance, a manoeuvre that did not escape the keen observation of Lady Ashworth.

“I quite agree, Lady Ashworth. And Miss Vance, I must ask, have you had occasion to visit the new exhibition of watercolours at the Gallery? It is, I hear, quite a remarkable collection, though some critics find the colours rather too bold for the delicate subject matter.” He clearly hoped to draw her into a more personal exchange, away from the general pronouncements of their companions.

“I have not yet had the pleasure,” Miss Vance admitted, a slight flush rising to her cheeks, for she felt the intensity of his gaze rather unsettling. “My time has been much occupied with the ordering of a small library, a task which, whilst pleasant enough, demands a certain solitude. But I mean to go, certainly, before the exhibition concludes. Do you commend it yourself, Mr. Finch?”

“Most highly, Miss Vance, most highly,” he replied, appearing quite pleased with her question. “Though I should confess, my judgment may be somewhat biased; I confess to having purchased a small piece myself, a charming vignette of the Italian countryside. I have it with me, in fact, and would be delighted to show it to you, if you would but indulge my vanity.” He gestured towards a leather portfolio lying on a side table.

Mrs. Pemberton clapped her hands with genuine delight. “Oh, a new acquisition! How very exciting! Mr. Finch’s taste, you must know, is quite impeccable, Miss Vance. He has the most wonderful eye for art. We must all see it at once, must we not, Lady Ashworth?”

Lady Ashworth merely gave a brief, almost imperceptible nod, her eyes still fixed on her embroidery, though Miss Vance suspected little escaped her notice. Miss Vance, however, felt a sudden apprehension. To view a purchase of Mr. Finch’s, in such a company, felt perilously close to an intimacy she did not desire, especially given his pointed attention. She sought for a polite refusal, but before she could formulate one, Mr. Finch had already risen and was retrieving the portfolio. He returned, holding it carefully, and presented it with an air of modest triumph. “It is but a trifle, of course, but I believe it captures a certain melancholic beauty, an essence of faded grandeur one rarely encounters in these modern times.”

He unfolded the stiff paper, holding it towards Miss Vance first. The watercolour depicted a ruined Roman arch, shrouded in ivy, with a shepherd and his flock in the foreground. It was undeniably well-executed, if a trifle conventional in its romanticism. Miss Vance murmured her polite appreciation, though she was conscious of Lady Ashworth’s steady, discerning gaze upon the image, and upon herself.

“Indeed, it is quite charming,” Mrs. Pemberton exclaimed, leaning in perhaps a little too closely. “Such fine detail, Mr. Finch! One can almost feel the moss underfoot. You have truly an exquisite eye.”

Mr. Finch beamed, clearly satisfied. “I endeavour, Mrs. Pemberton, to cultivate an appreciation for the beautiful, wherever it may be found. And Miss Vance, do you not agree that the perspective here, the way the light catches the distant hills, speaks to a particular solitude, a meditative quality one seldom finds amidst the bustle of London?” His query was aimed solely at her, a challenge to discern a deeper meaning.

Eleanor felt a pressure to offer something beyond simple admiration. She paused, considering, wishing to avoid any appearance of either being overly impressed or overly dismissive. “It certainly evokes a strong sense of tranquil isolation,” she observed carefully, “though I confess, my own preference often lies with landscapes that suggest more human activity, a visible connection to everyday life. There is a certain melancholy in ruins, however beautifully rendered, that sometimes leaves me desiring a livelier scene.”

Mr. Finch’s smile faltered, just for a moment, before he recovered himself with a slight cough. “Ah, a preference for the animated, then? I understand perfectly, Miss Vance. Though I must contend that even in quiet contemplation there is a profound animation of the spirit. But perhaps I am too much the philosopher this afternoon.” He glanced briefly at Lady Ashworth, whose lips were now pressed into a thin line, betraying, Miss Vance thought, a quiet amusement at Mr. Finch’s slight discomfiture. It was clear that Eleanor’s gentle critique, however courteously delivered, had not been precisely the adulation Mr. Finch had expected, nor indeed, that which he often received. The room settled into a moment of comfortable silence, broken only by the faint click of Lady Ashworth’s needle against her thimble.
